report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: A REM Model of Collaborative Recognition Memory

text.text: Recognition memory is often studied as an individual process, yet many recognition decisions are made collaboratively.
Collaborative recognition requires individuals to communicate and combine separate, imperfect memory evidence to reach a joint decision.
Here, we develop a computational model of collaborative recognition memory (CO-REM) grounded in the well-established Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model of individual recognition.
We compare collaborative decision rules based on categorical old/new decisions, confidence judgments, and the direct integration of memory evidence.

The simulations show that groups can outperform even their best individual member, but the benefits depend on differences in individual recognition ability and how memory evidence is communicated and combined.
Confidence sharing can produce collective gains or losses depending on how individuals map their memory evidence onto confidence judgments.

The model also predicts greater collaborative benefits for recognizing previously studied items (targets) than for correctly rejecting new items (lures), consistent with some previous empirical findings.

Although the predicted performance differences are small, CO-REM provides a framework for identifying the conditions under which collaboration improves recognition and for guiding future empirical investigations.
Memory is often treated as an individual cognitive process, but many important memory judgments are made collaboratively.
Witnesses discuss what they saw.
Medical teams decide whether a current case resembles prior cases.
Students answer questions together.
Analysts judge whether a new event matches a known pattern.
In these cases, and others, it is important to know when and whether collaboration improves memory or distorts it.
Conventional wisdom tells us that "two heads are better than one."
Empirically, this wisdom sometimes holds.
For instance, Mellers et al. (2014) found that placing expert forecasters in groups to share information and discuss rationales improved the accuracy of geopolitical forecasts.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Mellers et al. (2014)</ref> found that placing expert forecasters in groups to share information and discuss rationales improved the accuracy of geopolitical forecasts.

text.text: Yet collaboration can also impair judgment, as in groupthink, when cohesive groups prioritize consensus, harmony, or loyalty over critical evaluation of alternatives (Janis, 1982).
text.formatted: Yet collaboration can also impair judgment, as in groupthink, when cohesive groups prioritize consensus, harmony, or loyalty over critical evaluation of alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Janis, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: These different outcomes suggest that group performance depends on the social and cognitive mechanisms by which individuals collaborate to form a collective judgment (Kameda et al., 2022; Kerr & Tindale, 2004; Kozlowski & Ilgen, 2006).
text.formatted: These different outcomes suggest that group performance depends on the social and cognitive mechanisms by which individuals collaborate to form a collective judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kameda et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kerr & Tindale, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kozlowski & Ilgen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Prior work has emphasized several such mechanisms, including how groups sample shared versus uniquely held information (Lu et al., 2012; Stasser & Abele, 2020; Stasser & Titus, 1985), how cohesion, goals, and norms shape members' motivation and attention to task-relevant information (Evans & Dion, 1991; Mullen & Copper, 1994; Podsakoff et al., 1997), and how aggregation rules combine individual judgments into a collective response (Hastie & Kameda, 2005; Sorkin et al., 1998).

text.text: Altogether, these results reveal that collaboration produces gains or losses in performance not simply because multiple people are involved, but because interaction changes what information is expressed, how it is evaluated, and how it is integrated into a collective judgment.
Collaborative memory-when people form and retrieve memories in the company of others (Rajaram, 2024; Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2010)-adds an important complication to this general picture.
text.formatted: Collaborative memory-when people form and retrieve memories in the company of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rajaram, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2010)</ref>-adds an important complication to this general picture.

text.text: During collaborative memory, particularly at retrieval, individuals often bring to the group not an explicit fact or stable judgment, but an internal memory signal or information derived from it.

This information may be the recalled item itself, partial recollection, familiarity, uncertainty, or confidence that an event occurred (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968; Nelson & Shiffrin, 2013; Kahana & Wagner, 2024).
text.formatted: This information may be the recalled item itself, partial recollection, familiarity, uncertainty, or confidence that an event occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Nelson & Shiffrin, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kahana & Wagner, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: During collaboration, these internal states must be translated into something shareable.

Group performance, thus, depends not only on how individual responses are aggregated, but also on which aspects of memory evidence are expressed, how diagnostic those expressions are, and how they are integrated with the evidence supplied by others (Rajaram, 2024; Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2010).
text.formatted: Group performance, thus, depends not only on how individual responses are aggregated, but also on which aspects of memory evidence are expressed, how diagnostic those expressions are, and how they are integrated with the evidence supplied by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rajaram, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This effect of how memory evidence is expressed and integrated has been primarily studied in collaborative free recall.
Here, individuals interact in groups of two or more to recall as many previously studied items as possible.

Although conventional wisdom would suggest that that groups remember more, surprisingly, groups recall fewer nonredundant items than nominal groups formed by pooling the separate recall of the same number of individuals (Basden et al., 1997; Gates et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2008; Marion & Thorley, 2016; Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2010; Weldon & Bellinger, 1997).

text.text: By analogy, in collaborative recall, one group member's output may act as externally imposed cues that disrupt another member's preferred retrieval strategy, reducing access to items that might have been recalled when working alone.

text.text: Collaborative recognition, the topic of this paper, raises a related but distinct problem.

In a typical collaborative recognition task, individuals study a common set of items and are later presented with test probes that must be jointly classified as "old" or "new" (Clark et al., 2000 (Clark et al., , 2006;; Hinsz, 1990; Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2007; Vollrath et al., 1989).
text.formatted: In a typical collaborative recognition task, individuals study a common set of items and are later presented with test probes that must be jointly classified as "old" or "new" <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Clark et al., 2000</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clark et al., , 2006;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hinsz, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Vollrath et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike free recall, the candidate item is supplied by the test itself.
Collaborators therefore evaluate the same external retrieval cue, reducing the chance that one person's response will disrupt another person's memory search.

Collaborative recognition has not been studied very often, but the results suggest that collaboration facilitates rather than inhibits performance (Clark et al., 2000; Hinsz, 1990; Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin, 2007; Vollrath et al., 1989).

text.text: Importantly, this advantage does not appear to be reducible to simple vote counting over independent old/new decisions. Clark et al. (2000) found that, for three-person groups, collaborative recognition exceeded what could be achieved by majority processes alone, suggesting that discussion contributed information beyond the separate votes of individual members. Rajaram and Pereira-Pasarin (2007) also found that discussion improved later individual recognition even when participants did not produce a single consensus response, indicating that collaborative benefits can arise from the exchange of memory-relevant information rather than from the final response rule alone.

text.text: If collaborative recognition is not simply the aggregation of categorical old/new decisions, then collaborators may be exchanging or using richer information.

Work on joint perceptual decision making has addressed an analogous problem by comparing computational models that differ in the information observers share when forming a joint decision about a common perceptual stimulus (e.g., identifying a higher-contrast Gabor patch; Bahrami et al., 2010) (see also Koriat, 2012). Bahrami et al. showed that when collaborators have similar perceptual discriminability, dyads can outperform their better members and approach the performance predicted by models in which richer information is shared.

text.text: Critically, both their model and empirical results showed that this advantage declines as collaborators' abilities diverge: when one observer was substantially less sensitive than the other, dyads no longer reliably outperformed the better individual, and in many cases performed worse.
Their account emphasized confidence as the information used to combine individual judgments.
When collaborators have similar abilities, confidence provides a reasonably comparable signal of the strength of their evidence.

As their abilities diverge, however, equally strong confidence can give the poorer performer too much influence because confidence is expressed relative to each observer's own internal evidence and uncertainty (see also Koriat, 2012).

text.text: We draw on this work asking if and how similar dynamics might shape collaborative recognition memory.
To investigate collaborative recognition, we use the Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: To investigate collaborative recognition, we use the Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: REM is a global-matching model of recognition memory.
It represents recognition evidence as a graded-likelihood signal: odds a test item is old vs new.

Although recognition decisions can involve both familiarity and recall (e.g. Yonelinas, 2002), the decisions based on these are often highly correlated making a familiarity-based model sufficient for the present purposes (e.g. Dunn, 2008).

text.text: We can then specify different collaborative rules in which individuals share only categorical old/new decisions, confidence-like transformations of their evidence, or the underlying memory evidence itself.
Our research focused on three linked questions.
First, under what conditions does collaborative recognition exceed or fall below the best individual?
Second, motivated by the findings from Clark et al. (2000), under what conditions can collaboration benefit targets more than lures and why?
text.formatted: Second, motivated by the findings from <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Clark et al. (2000)</ref>, under what conditions can collaboration benefit targets more than lures and why?

text.text: Finally, do the same boundary conditions hold in larger groups?
We address this by defining the evidence available to each collaborative rule and comparing its predictions as group members' encoding quality varies.
A simulation-first approach helps because collaborative recognition experiments can make the effects of different information-sharing rules hard to isolate.
For example, when collaborators agree on a recognition decision before discussing or sharing information, the group is unlikely to change it.
Moreover, different instructions and communication procedures may induce different forms of information sharing.

Rather than examining each combination empirically, the simulations allow us to identify the conditions under which collaborative gains or losses should occur and thereby guide the design of subsequent experiments.
Our modeling framework has two layers.
The first layer starts with the well-established global-matching model of recognition memory, REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).

text.text: REM is useful for the present purposes because it provides a mechanistic account of recognition decisions in which memory probes are compared against noisy, incomplete item traces and converted into likelihood-ratio evidence for an old-versus-new response (the odds).
Each individual, alone or in a group, is assumed to start by obtaining an odds value and a decision based on it.
The second layer consists of collaboration rules that let group members reach a joint decision based on what they can communicate to others and how they combine that information.
We develop each in turn next.
We refer to the full model as Collaborative REM, or CO-REM.
We first describe the individual REM process and then turn to the collaboration rules.
REM is a global match model of recognition memory (Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Raaijmakers & Shiffrin, 2002).
text.formatted: REM is a global match model of recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Clark & Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Raaijmakers & Shiffrin, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Like other global-matching models, REM posits recognition to depend on the match between a test probe and the contents of memory.
It was designed to produce optimal decisions derived from its few assumptions.
On this basis, it provides a likelihood ratio, called odds, of an item being old vs. new.
If targets and lures occur equally often, an "Old" decision is made when the odds are greater than 1.0.

Note that the decision variable in REM is not raw familiarity or summed similarity as in some global match models (e.g., Hintzman, 1988; Raaijmakers & Shiffrin, 2002), but diagnostic evidence for an old response relative to a new response.

The value of each feature is a positive integer representing the base-rate frequency of that feature in the natural environment, in the task setting, or both.

The parameter g controls the base-rate distribution of feature values.
Larger values of g place more probability on small, common feature values, whereas smaller values of g spread probability toward larger, rarer feature values.
Assume that N items are studied.
When each item is studied, REM stores an episodic image of that item.
The image is incomplete and error-prone.
Each feature is stored independently with probability u, the storage probability.
If a feature is not stored, its value is represented by zero.
Conditional on storage, the correct feature value is copied with probability c (the copy probability); otherwise, the stored value is sampled from the base-rate distribution.

For retrieval, the vector of 20 feature values representing the tested item, called the probe, is compared position by position with the stored vector of non-zero values for each item stored in memory, termed images.

text.text: REM provides a useful foundation for the present work because it has been used to explain several benchmark findings in recognition memory.

These include a variety of mirror effects by which the better recognized class of items has both higher hit rates (probability of an old response to a target) and lower false-alarm rates (probability of an old response to a foil), compared with the class of items less well recognized.
The prime example is word-frequency:

Low-frequency words often produce both higher hit rates and lower false-alarm rates than highfrequency words (Glanzer et al., 1993; Glanzer & Adams, 1985; Malmberg et al., 2002; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).

There are two versions of this model that depend on the basis for the agent's formation of a confidence rating.
The two versions differ in how internal odds evidence is mapped onto a confidence rating.
In this version of the MC model, termed relative (MCR), the three confidence levels depend solely on an agent's personal odds.

Thus, an agent with very poor memory might have generally low odds on all tests but still give a high rating for what might be a low absolute odds value; this happens when that low value is in the high range for that agent.

Conversely, an agent with excellent memory might have generally high odds on all tests but still give a low confidence rating for a high absolute odds value; this happens when that high value falls in the low range for that agent.

higher log odds).
The simulations show when and how often these situations arise for agents with differing memory abilities.
In this MC model, termed absolute, so MCA, each agent learns, knows, and takes advantage of their own memory ability.
They, therefore, give three ratings that reflect the actual evidential value of their log odds.
An agent with excellent memory will therefore give mostly high ratings, and an agent with poor memory will give mostly low ratings.

Each replication contained 2,400 balanced test probes (1,200 OLD and 1,200 NEW), yielding 38,400 test probes per condition.
The primary measure of interest is overall accuracy, reported as the average of hit rate and correct-rejection rate.
We refer to this statistic as balanced accuracy.
Also reported are the separate predictions for hits and correct rejections.
These can be compared to the average performance of the agents making separate decisions (which in the simulations are the initial decisions before collaboration).
This comparison would be the same as comparing the other models to the guessing model.

For any of these measures of accuracy, we also compare the group performance to that of the agent who performs best overall (on all trials, measured by the overall average of hit and correct rejection rates).
This is reported by the collective benefit ratio, or CBR: dyad or triad accuracy divided by the accuracy of the best individual in that condition.
A ratio above 1 indicates a collective benefit; a ratio below 1 indicates performance below the best individual.

We used CO-REM to investigate collaborative recognition performance and in general how the different types of information people might share about their recognition during collaboration can impact performance.
For the purpose of this paper, we focus on five questions.
First, when can a dyad outperform its best member?
Second, when does confidence-based collaboration fail?
Third, why might collaborative benefits be stronger for targets than for distractors?
Fourth, does the same logic extend from dyads to triads?

And finally given the limited number of empirical studies on collaborative recognition and the challenges of designing and running studies of collaborative memory, what are the magnitudes and characteristics of the predicted effects?
We answer the first four questions in turn and address the fifth question about the characteristics of the effects as we answer the other four questions.
In our REM simulations, the agent's memory ability is manipulated by varying the correct-copy probability c, which determines the probability that the correct feature value is stored at study.
By varying c we effectively manipulate encoding quality and ultimately the recognition ability of the agent.

We focused our simulations on the copy probability c in the range [.1 .9] because more extreme abilities are unlikely in an empirical study, and because we wish to compare performance of the collaboration models to a model by which the choice on each trial is that of the best agent overall (thus requiring that the best agent be less than perfect and above chance).

In our simulations, we set this number to three.

The analysis reveals several observations.

Third, the right column shows that the main factor determining the performance of the absolute-evidence mapping and its deviation from OS is the large proportion of guesses that occur because the two agents report the same level of confidence, but this decreases as the number of ratings increases.

Instead, as we showed earlier, what impacts the relative-evidence mapping's performance is the high number of times the less accurate agent reports a high confidence on the disagreement trials.
Overall, the comparison shows that the way agents translate memory evidence into confidence reports shapes collaborative performance.

Collaboration gains or losses for groups of three (triads)
We next consider whether the patterns observed for dyads extend to triads.
An important difference between dyads and triads is that when two agents disagree, neither has a majority, but when three agents disagree, two members necessarily agree on a response.
Thus, majority voting provides a natural baseline for evaluating collaborative recognition.
Majority voting can produce a wisdom-of-crowd effect (Davis-Stober et al., 2014; Herzog et al., 2019).

To do so, we extended the CO-REM collaboration rules to triads.
Each agent first makes an individual old/new decision.
When all three agree, the group retains that decision.
Otherwise, the majority-voting model (MV) adapts the response of the two agreeing members.
In the confidence sharing models (MCA and MCR), the group instead follows the decision of the member reporting the highest confidence.
When the highest confidence rating is shared by members making opposing decisions, the majority decision takes precedence.
Thus, a lone dissenter can override the majority only when reporting strictly higher confidence than both other members.
As in the dyadic models, confidence ratings are treated as ordered categories rather than quantities to be integrated.
In contrast, the OS model integrates the continuous log-likelihood evidence from all three agents.
These rules allow us to compare majority voting, categorical confidence sharing, and the integration of continuous memory evidence in triads.

Several patterns emerge.
First, the OS model consistently exceeds the best individual, providing an upper benchmark for collective performance.
Second, majority voting does not necessarily outperform the best individual, particularly when members differ substantially in recognition ability.
Third, both MCA and MCR can outperform majority voting and the best individual, with MCA generally performing better than MCR.
The benefits depend not simply on how similar the members are in ability, but also on the distribution of abilities within the group.
For example, even when one member has relatively poor memory, a triad containing two stronger members can benefit from sharing confidence.

text.text: Across the simulated conditions, approximately 68% of the trials produced a 2-1 split.
Of these trials, MCR overturned the majority 17.5% of the time compared with 15.0% for MCA.
However, only 59% of MCR's overturns were correct, compared with 73% for MCA.
Consequently, MCR improved balance accuracy by about 2 percentage points whereas MCA improved it by nearly 5 percentage points.
The difference between the models is attributable to the degree confidence reflects individual recognition ability.
Under MCR, each member uses the confidence categories equally often, regardless of their memory ability, giving weaker members similar opportunities to override the majority.
Under MCA, confidence better reflects the diagnostic value of each member's evidence, so overturns are more likely to come from the stronger member and to be correct.
Thus, as in dyads, the benefits of sharing confidence depend on how well confidence communicates the underlying memory evidence.
Whether we are trying to identify a familiar face, determine if an event occurred, or judge whether we have heard something before, we often rely on others to help make those recognition decisions.
Underlying such collaboration is the belief that "two heads are better than one."
Yet, collaborating during recognition decisions introduces its own challenges.
Each person brings separate, imperfect memory evidence to the decision and must find a way to communicate that evidence to others.
The group must then find a way to use the shared information to reach a common decision.
In this paper, we developed CO-REM to examine how different forms of information sharing shape collaborative recognition performance.
CO-REM builds on the well-established REM model of individual recognition memory, which represents memory evidence as a likelihood ratio favoring an old or new response (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: CO-REM builds on the well-established REM model of individual recognition memory, which represents memory evidence as a likelihood ratio favoring an old or new response <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: We used this model to investigate several ways individuals may make collaborative recognition decisions from sharing categorical old/new recognition decisions to confidence judgments to the direct integration of memory evidence.
The simulations show that indeed that two heads can be better than one, with collaborating agents outperforming the best individual member, a so-called "assembly bonus effect" (Kerr & Tindale, 2004).
text.formatted: The simulations show that indeed that two heads can be better than one, with collaborating agents outperforming the best individual member, a so-called "assembly bonus effect" <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kerr & Tindale, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, this benefit depends on the recognition abilities of the individuals and how they communicate and use their memory evidence.
In general, the collective benefit is greatest when individuals have similar recognition abilities and decreases as their abilities diverge, even when their memory evidence is optimally integrated.
With more limited forms of information sharing, group performance can even fall below that of the best individual.
Our primary hypothesis is that during collaborative recognition, people communicate the strength of their memory evidence via confidence.

This hypothesis aligns with our understanding of metacognition (Nelson & Narens, 1994), communication of uncertainty (Wallsten & Budescu, 1995), and collaborative perceptual decision making (Bahrami et al., 2010; Bang et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This hypothesis aligns with our understanding of metacognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Nelson & Narens, 1994)</ref>, communication of uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Wallsten & Budescu, 1995)</ref>, and collaborative perceptual decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bahrami et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bang et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Our simulations suggest that how individuals map their memory evidence onto confidence judgment can substantially affect collaborative performance.
When confidence is expressed relative to each person's own evidence distribution, weaker members can exert too much influence over the collective decision.
In contrast, when confidence more directly reflects the diagnostic value of memory evidence, collaborative performance generally improves.
It is interesting to contrast our results with the better-studied case of collaborative recall.

In free recall, as we established, collaborating groups demonstrate collaborative inhibition where they typically recall fewer items than nominal groups formed by pooling the responses of individuals working separately (Basedn et al., 1997; Weldon & Bellinger, 1997).
text.formatted: In free recall, as we established, collaborating groups demonstrate collaborative inhibition where they typically recall fewer items than nominal groups formed by pooling the responses of individuals working separately <ref type="bibr">(Basedn et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Weldon & Bellinger, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: This inhibition is thought to occur because hearing others' responses disrupts an individual's own retrieval strategy.
Collaborative recognition differs because the test item is provided, reducing the likelihood of any retrieval disruption.
Instead, as CO-REM illustrates, collaborators must decide how to use the memory evidence each person generates in response to the same probe.
Our simulations suggest that this creates collaboration to improve recognition, but also the possibility of poorer performance when individuals less diagnostic evidence have too much influence.
Thus, instead of disruptions of retrieval, the benefits and costs of collaborative recognition may depend more heavily on how individuals communicate and combine their memory evidence.
As we noted in the introduction, in this paper we adopted a simulation approach to better understand the basic aspects of collaborative recognition and to identify clear predictions.
To this end, CO-REM makes several predictions that may guide future research.
One is that collaboration can produce greater benefits for recognizing previously studied items (targets) than for correctly rejecting new items (lures).

In CO-REM this asymmetry arises from the skewed distributions of the evidence where memory evidence sometimes is particularly strong for target items, which in collaborative recognition creates opportunities for one member's evidence to correct another member's error.
Consistent with this prediction, Cark et al. (2000) reported such an asymmetry with stronger collaborative facilitation for targets than for distractors.
text.formatted: Consistent with this prediction, <ref type="bibr">Cark et al. (2000)</ref> reported such an asymmetry with stronger collaborative facilitation for targets than for distractors.

text.text: Another prediction is that gains and losses should vary systematically with differences in individual recognition ability and the composition of the group.
These predictions suggest several ways to investigate collaborative recognition empirically.
One approach would be to first assess individual recognition ability and then form dyads whose members have similar or different abilities.
During a subsequent collaborative recognition task, each participant could first make an independent old/new decision and confidence judgment before the dyad reaches a joint decision.
The different dyad compositions would test the prediction of when there is a gain or loss from collective recognition.

Furthermore, manipulating whether participants communicate only their categorical decisions or also their confidence, can help test how information sharing and group composition jointly affect recognition performance.
We could also manipulate feedback to learn if and how the calibration of confidence ratings might change could help distinguish relative from absolute confidence sharing.
Finally, CO-REM simulations suggest the predicted differences are generally small, which implies the experiments will need a high number of trials to test these predictions.
When it comes to collaborative recognition, two heads can indeed be better than one when making recognition decisions, but the benefits of collaboration are not guaranteed.
